To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
effective connectivity from the early visual cortex to the posterior occipital face areas gives rise and predicts face selectivity.

feedforward connectivity from early visual areas to face-selective posterior occipittemporal areas is important in generating face selectivity in these face areas and that reduced feedforward connectivity is related to the diminished face-selectivity in the face areas of people with developmental prosognosia.

effective connectivity from EVC to face-selective areas gives rise to cortical face selectivity, and that reduced effective connectivity between early and posterior occitopital face areas predicts face recognition impairment in people with DP.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural basis of face selectivity and the mechanisms underlying developmental prosopagnosis.
how face selectivity emerges in the brain, what factors contribute to this selectivity, and what happens when face selectivity fails to emerge.
how face recognition is achieved and how it is affected in individuals with face recognition impairment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

effective connectivity from the early visual cortex to the face-selective regions in the posterior occitotemporal cortex gives rise to face-selective responses, and that reduced connectivity from the early to the posterior occipital cortex predicts reduced face-selectivity in developmental prosopagnosa.
effective connectivity from EVC to occipital face areas, EVC to fusiform face area, and EVC-pSTS best explains how face selectivity emerges in both controls and DP.

effective connectivity between early visual cortex and posterior occipitopetal face areas gives rise and maintains face selectivity in posterior occipitoptemporal face areas, and reduced face selectivity and effective connectivity in this network predicts developmental prosopagnosa.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

face selectivity arises from effective connectivity from early sensory cortex to posterior occitoparietal areas, and that this connectivity is reduced in individuals with face recognition impairments.

the face-selective regions are not face-selective per se but rather become face-selective by receiving feedforward projections from the early visual cortex carrying face information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
face selectivity is a consequence of the effective connectivity between brain areas, and not the result of the activity of a single face-selective area.

the generation of face selectivity and the neural abnormalities associated with developmental prosopagnosis can both be explained by the effective connectivity from early to posterior face processing areas.
